title: Improving Large-scale Language Models and Resources for Filipino
venue: Proceedings of the Thirteenth Language Resources and Evaluation Conference (LREC 2022)
problem_statement: Low-resource languages such as Filipino suffer from a severe scarcity of benchmark datasets, linguistic tools, and large-scale pretrained language models, which impedes NLP research progress. Prior Filipino language models (such as Tagalog BERT and ELECTRA) were pretrained on small, topically narrow corpora like WikiText-TL-39, resulting in sub-optimal downstream performance on complex classification tasks and limiting the capacity of larger transformer architectures.
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Filipino / Tagalog Language Modeling, Low-Resource Languages, Text Classification, Pretraining Corpus Construction
theoretical_framework: Self-supervised Transformer language modeling and the RoBERTa robust optimization framework (Liu et al., 2019) building upon BERT masked language modeling (Devlin et al., 2018); Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) subword tokenization (Sennrich et al., 2015); memory-efficient optimization via Adafactor (Shazeer and Stern, 2018); and inverted-pyramid discourse entailing structures for natural language inference generation (Cruz et al., 2021).
methodology: The authors construct TLUnified, a large-scale, topically diverse Filipino pretraining corpus, by aggregating and deduplicating diverse Filipino text sources including bilingual bitexts (e.g., bible-uedin, CCAligned, ParaCrawl, TED2020, WikiMatrix, OpenSubtitles), the deduplicated Filipino split of OSCAR, and a 60% subset of the NewsPH news corpus. Raw text is cleaned using five deterministic filters: non-Latin character threshold (>15% non-Latin removed), sentence token length bounds (4 <= N <= 150), consecutive punctuation filtering, average word length ratio bounds (3 <= r <= 18), and HTML/URL artifact removal, followed by deduplication. A 32,000 BPE subword tokenizer with character coverage 1.0 is trained without uncasing. Using TLUnified, the authors pretrain two RoBERTa variants—Base (110M parameters, 12 layers, 768 hidden, 100k steps, lr=6e-4) and Large (330M parameters, 24 layers, 1024 hidden, 300k steps, lr=4e-4)—using Adafactor on 8x NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPUs with dynamic batching up to 8,192 tokens. The models are evaluated by finetuning with Adafactor on three downstream Filipino classification benchmarks: 2016 Election Hate Speech Detection, Dengue Infoveillance multi-label classification (reformulated as 32-class classification), and NewsPH-NLI Medium (generated from the unexposed 40% NewsPH split).
datasets: TLUnified: A large-scale pretraining corpus for Filipino constructed by combining deduplicated Filipino text from bitext corpora (bible-uedin, CCAligned, ELRC 2922, MultiC-CAligned, ParaCrawl, TED2020, WikiMatrix, tico-19, Ubuntu, OpenSubtitles, QED, Tanzil, Tatoeba, GlobalVoices, KDE4, WikiMedia), OSCAR Tagalog split, and 60% of NewsPH
Filipino Hatespeech Dataset: 10,000 Philippine presidential election-related tweets from 2016 annotated for binary hate speech classification (Cabasag et al., 2019)
Filipino Dengue Dataset: 4,000 low-resource disease infoveillance tweets annotated across 5 binary health labels, transformed into a 32-class single-label classification task (Livelo and Cheng, 2018)
NewsPH-NLI Medium: An entailment benchmark dataset generated from the remaining 40% unseen subset of the NewsPH news corpus to evaluate natural language inference without pretraining data leakage
WikiText-TL-39: Previous small-scale Filipino Wikipedia pretraining corpus used as a historical baseline comparison (Cruz and Cheng, 2019)
key_findings: RoBERTa models pretrained on TLUnified substantially outperform previous Filipino transformer baselines (Tagalog BERT and ELECTRA) across all three evaluation benchmarks, achieving an average gain of 4.47% test accuracy.

RoBERTa Large achieves the highest test accuracy across all tasks: 72.67% on Hate Speech (+4.07% over BERT Base), 90.00% on Dengue (+5.30% over BERT Base), and 91.09% on NewsPH-NLI Medium (+4.04% over ELECTRA Base).
RoBERTa Base demonstrates strong performance improvements (+3.90% on Hate Speech, +4.40% on Dengue, and +3.95% on NewsPH-NLI Medium over baselines), closely trailing RoBERTa Large.

The performance gap between RoBERTa Base and RoBERTa Large is marginal (+0.17% on Hate Speech, +0.90% on Dengue, and +0.09% on NewsPH-NLI Medium), indicating that while TLUnified improves significantly upon WikiText-TL-39, larger corpora are required to fully saturate and exploit the parameter capacity of large-scale 330M transformer models.

Non-destructive preprocessing preserving capitalization, casing, and adding task-specific tokens ([LINK], [MENTION], [HASHTAG]) with averaged subword embedding initialization maintains vital morphological and syntactic cues in noisy social media text.
scope_and_delimitations: The pretraining dataset TLUnified and resulting RoBERTa models focus exclusively on the Filipino (Tagalog) language, excluding other Philippine regional languages.
Evaluation is delimited to three specific classification tasks: binary hate speech detection, 32-class dengue infoveillance classification, and natural language inference.

Model architecture scope is delimited to masked language modeling via RoBERTa (Base with 110M parameters and Large with 330M parameters), without evaluating autoregressive decoder-only or sequence-to-sequence models.
To prevent data contamination and artificial performance inflation, NewsPH-NLI Medium was generated exclusively from a 40% split of NewsPH that was withheld from TLUnified pretraining.
Finetuning sequence lengths were truncated to 256 subwords for Base and Large models to reduce memory and training time, as no downstream sentence or sentence pair exceeded 256 subwords.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: The difference in performance between the Base and Large RoBERTa variants is marginal in the current benchmarks. Large outperforms Base only by +0.17% for Hatespeech, +0.9% for Dengue, and +0.09% for NewsPH-NLI Medium. We hypothesize that this is due to the size of the pretraining dataset. While the size of TLUnified is much larger than the previous WikiText-TL-39, it may still not be enough to make full use of the capacity of a Large-variant Transformer. We surmise that RoBERTa Large may need to be trained with more data to show significant, non-marginal improvements in performance.
limitations.summary: The authors acknowledge that the performance improvement of RoBERTa Large over RoBERTa Base is marginal across the evaluated benchmarks (between +0.09% and +0.90% accuracy). They attribute this bottleneck to pretraining corpus size, noting that although TLUnified is substantially larger and more diverse than WikiText-TL-39, the corpus remains insufficient to fully realize the representational capacity of large 330M-parameter Transformer models.

generalizability_gap: TLUnified and the pretrained RoBERTa models cover only standard Filipino/Tagalog text, leaving unexamined the more than 170 other regional Philippine languages (such as Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon, and Waray) as well as heavy conversational code-switching (Taglish) and generative language modeling capabilities.
methodological_gap: Evaluation was restricted to three sentence- and tweet-level classification tasks, lacking evaluation on generative NLP tasks (such as machine translation, summarization, and question answering) or token-level sequence labeling tasks (such as named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging). In addition, pretraining data volume constraints prevented RoBERTa Large from demonstrating substantial capacity scaling gains over RoBERTa Base.
future_work: Scaling pretraining data beyond TLUnified to enable large-scale Transformer models to realize their full parameter capacity.
Expanding Filipino language model evaluations to broader downstream tasks, including sequence labeling, question answering, and text generation.
Exploring multilingual and regional pretraining adaptations for other under-resourced Philippine languages.
